abstract_summary: Traditional large language models (LLMs) are scoped to individual user sessions, limiting their knowledge to a single conversation and preventing them from learning user preferences that evolve over time. Existing agentic memory systems address this limitation but generally operate at the individual-user level, rest...

scholarly_quality.concise_summary: The paper presents a coherent systems/methods contribution: a privacy-aware, multi-agent, multi-user memory framework with a new benchmark. The contribution is clearly scoped, the method is formally specified, and the evaluation includes multiple models, domains, and metrics. The central claims about visibility classification and multi-user access control are supported by reported results, while operation accuracy is modest and retrieval relevance is weak. The authors explicitly acknowledge these limitations and provide detailed benchmark construction and validation procedures. The paper is methodologically transparent and appropriately positioned relative to prior work.

Memory Architectures for LLM Agents.Generative Agents [Park et al., 2023] introduced
the foundational agent memory architecture combining observation, reflection, and planning with
retrieval weighted by recency, importance, and relevance. The CoALA framework [Sumers et al.,
2024] formalized these ideas into a taxonomy decomposing agents into working, episodic, semantic,
and procedural memory modules. MemGPT [Packer et al., 2023] pioneered an OS-inspired tiered
memory with self-directed paging between main context and external storage. Subsequent work
has improved memory structure and maintenance. A-MEM [Xu et al., 2025] enables autonomous
memory reorganization across tasks. Mem0 [Chhikara et al., 2025] introduces a production-oriented
pipeline where the LLM selects among ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, and NOOP operations with
91% lower latency versus full-context baselines. MemInsight [Salama et 
[… separate evidence block …]
may simultaneously require both a memory write and a retrieval, whereas prior
pipelines (e.g., Mem0) assume exactly one operation per turn. The result is, to our knowledge, the
first end-to-end pipeline that unifies LLM-based extraction, automatic privacy classification, and
index-level access enforcement in a single modular, system-agnostic service.
Agent Memory Benchmarks.In terms of existing agent memory benchmarks, MemoryAgent-
Bench [Hu et al., 2025] evaluates memory retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding,
and selective forgetting in single-agent settings. LOCOMO [Maharana et al., 2024] provides a

Our evaluation has several limitations. First, tag overlap (35.5% on the best model; full results in
Table 2) is notably lower than other content metrics, suggesting that AIM's tag extraction strategy
needs refinement. Additionally, retrieval relevance peaks at 45.0% (Table 2). Lastly, our LOCOMO
evaluation (Table 5) uses a single pass, whereas Mem0 reports averages over 10 runs. This could
reduce statistical significance of claims. Additionally, LOCOMO is a single-user benchmark and does
not exercise AIM's multi-user privacy classification or cross-agent synchronization—the features
that most differentiate it from existing systems. Further work must be conducted to improve memory
retrieval, such as changing the number of retrieved memories before filtering.

positive_signals: The memory lifecycle is formally specified with a visibility predicate, multi-label intent detection, structured extraction, scope-restricted deduplication, and cascaded retrieval.
AIM is evaluated across five models, four domains, and multiple metrics with three independent runs, reporting visibility classification accuracy up to 96.0%.
The central privacy claim is supported by high visibility classification accuracy and deterministic index-level filtering.
The paper positions AIM against prior single-user memory systems and identifies the gap in multi-user access control and cross-agent synchronization.
The benchmark construction, validation guidelines, and evaluation methodology are documented in detail, supporting reproducibility.
The authors explicitly acknowledge limitations in tag extraction, retrieval relevance, LOCOMO comparison methodology, and public memory integrity.
The paper provides formal notation, equations, tables, and an algorithm, contributing to precise technical communication.
scholarly_quality.rationale: Evidence references failed manuscript-context validation; the proposed scientific judgment is withheld pending review.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The evaluation relies on a synthetic, LLM-generated benchmark with manual validation, so generalizability to real-world multi-user deployments is uncertain. Retrieval relevance is low (45.0% best), and tag overlap is weak, indicating core retrieval components are not yet strong. The LOCOMO comparison uses a single run versus Mem0's ten runs, limiting statistical confidence. The paper does not report direct measurement of private-memory leakage under adversarial queries beyond visibility classification accuracy, so the strongest privacy guarantee is inferred from the index-level predicate rather than empirically demonstrated end-to-end.
